### Idea

In the trail-running podcast The Albon Way, I heard John Albon describe training as a card-based system. It immediately clicked with me.

I had a clear idea of what the cards should be, but not yet how everything around them would work. I wanted that part to take shape as we built, letting the original card idea guide the project.

I could vividly picture the idea of running training cards, and I wanted to turn that picture into something real. The concept was to create a set of training cards, a bit like Pokémon, Yu-Gi-Oh, or Cars cards, but built specifically for running. Each card would capture something practical about a training element, such as what exactly to do, its strengths, what it does, when to use it, and who it is for.

Those cards would not just be loose notes. I had a very clear picture of how they could look and work, and that visual idea appealed to me a lot. I wanted them to follow a clear underlying structure while still appearing as real cards in a clean and intuitive user experience. In my head, it was something that could live inside an application and feel easy to browse, almost like a small training deck you could choose from naturally.

The reason this idea appealed to me is that training decisions can be mentally tiring. I usually know roughly where I am in a training period, but after a full day of work I do not always want to think too much about what the next session should be. I wanted this to become a quick tool that would reduce decision fatigue, make daily training choices easier, and give me a few ready-made options to choose from. At the same time, it would educate me about training along the way and make it easier for both newer and more experienced athletes to think about training, effort, and purpose in a clearer way.

The goal was also not to write all of the training content by myself. Instead, I wanted to use an AI agent as a kind of specialized coach, guided by prompts and grounded in publications, training principles, and established endurance knowledge, to help prepare and structure the cards. That way, the training logic would come from a more expert-like source, while I focused on the infrastructure and the overall system.

In a way, the project became a mix of my own ideas, AI support, and careful supervision. A lot of the implementation came together with AI support, but the structure, the card system, and the direction were still strongly shaped by my input. I also wanted the whole thing to stay easy to maintain, adjust, and reuse over time, so the cards would not just live inside this repo, but could also be reused in other projects that would bring the to life. This repo holds the card content and outputs it in a structured, way using a class-based setup.

### The Specialized Endurance Coach

Throughout the project, we relied on a separate AI agent as our specialized endurance - (trail) running coach. We gave it a clear role through a set of detailed prompts and treated it as a coach working alongside us. Whenever the project involved endurance knowledge, we used it to provide the specialist information: from deciding what a useful card should contain and how the cards should work together, to defining their purpose and filling them with content.

In a way, we outsourced the endurance-specific knowledge to the coach while keeping responsibility for the idea, structure, infrastructure, and direction of the project. Its guidance was based on publications, established training systems, and common endurance-training principles, while we focused on turning that knowledge into a clear and usable system.

### Training Cards and Hierarchy

#### Hierarchy

Endurance training is usually organized into connected training blocks. Each block covers a different period and has its own purpose, while also containing smaller blocks within it. These are the blocks represented by the cards:

**Macro block** · *roughly several months* · Defines the main training phase.

<div style="margin-left: 2rem;">↓</div>

**Mezzo block** · *roughly several weeks* · Focuses on one part of that phase.

<div style="margin-left: 2rem;">↓</div>

**Micro block** · *roughly one week* · Organizes the training week.

<div style="margin-left: 2rem;">↓</div>

**Session** · *one workout* · Describes the individual training session.

The card structure follows this hierarchy. Each card is defined as a Python class based on its place in the training hierarchy. All card classes share the same *BaseTrainingCard*, which contains the information common to every card. The specialized *MacroCard*, *MezzoCard*, *MicroCard*, and *SessionCard* then build on that base by adding the fields needed for their own planning block.

#### BaseTrainingCard

`BaseTrainingCard` is the shared foundation for all card types. It creates the stable frame that every specialized card can build on.

It separates:

- What must always be there
- What is useful but not always present
- What only belongs to a specific card level

<details class="training-card-details">
<summary>BaseTrainingCard</summary>

```python
@dataclass(slots=True)
class BaseTrainingCard:
    id: str
    slug: str
    title: str
    card_type: CardType
    suitable_levels: list[TrainingLevel]
    summary: str
    purpose: str
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    philosophy_profile_ids: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    goal_race_context: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    training_profile: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    expected_adaptations: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    watchouts: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    progression_rules: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    regression_rules: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    additional_information: str = ""
    references: list[CardReference] = field(default_factory=list)
```

</details>

Using `slots=True` means that each card can only use the fields defined in its class. The card identity fields are `id`, `slug`, `title`, and `card_type`. In addition addition to the required fields `suitable_levels`, `summary`, and `purpose`, the other fields contain the card's coaching information, while `references` connects the card to other cards in the library.

Fields without a default value are required. Fields with a default value, such as `""` or `field(default_factory=list)`, can be left out when a card is created. They add detail without being necessary to identify the card. This keeps the schema balanced: strict enough to support consistent cards and coaching, but not so strict that writing cards becomes frustrating. Although `philosophy_profile_ids` has a default value in the class, validation still requires every valid card to contain at least one philosophy profile.

#### Specialized Card Classes

`MacroCard` represents the broadest planning block that spans over several weeks or more. It should help answer: what are we trying to accomplish during this phase, and how does it fit into the wider training plan?

It inherits the shared contract and adds the fields that matter only for a broad phase-level object.

<details class="training-card-details">
<summary>MacroCard</summary>

```python
@dataclass(slots=True)
class MacroCard(BaseTrainingCard):
    recommended_duration_weeks: str = ""
    timing_guidance: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
```

</details>

`MezzoCard` is the intermediate block layer. It answers: what are we sharpening inside this phase, and how should this block sit between the macro plan and the weekly load?

<details class="training-card-details">
<summary>MezzoCard</summary>

```python
@dataclass(slots=True)
class MezzoCard(BaseTrainingCard):
    recommended_duration_weeks: str = ""
    placement_guidance: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
```

</details>

`MicroCard` is the week-level planning card. It is the bridge between the block-level intention and the day-by-day reality of training. It describes how a coach shapes one training week to support the larger block.

<details class="training-card-details">
<summary>MicroCard</summary>

```python
@dataclass(slots=True)
class MicroCard(BaseTrainingCard):
    recommended_duration_days: str = ""
    week_structure: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    key_sessions: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    load_pattern: str = ""
    placement_guidance: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    recovery_requirements: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
```

</details>

`SessionCard` is the most detailed card. It describes one workout or session pattern. It needs enough structure to guide execution, but it should still feel like a reusable workout concept rather than a one-off prescription.

It is supported by three smaller classes: `WorkoutBlock`, `WorkoutOption`, and `SessionPart`. They break a workout into its main parts, possible variations, and individual instructions. `SessionFamily` groups similar workouts under a common label. Together, these supporting classes give each session a clear structure while still allowing us to represent different workout formats and options.

<details class="training-card-details">
<summary>SessionCard</summary>

```python
@dataclass(slots=True, kw_only=True)
class SessionCard(BaseTrainingCard):
    session_family: SessionFamily
    typical_duration: str = ""
    workout_blocks: list[WorkoutBlock] = field(default_factory=list)
```

</details>

<details class="training-card-details">
<summary>WorkoutBlock</summary>

```python
@dataclass(slots=True)
class WorkoutBlock:
    block_type: WorkoutBlockType
    execution_mode: WorkoutBlockExecutionMode = WorkoutBlockExecutionMode.DO_ALL
    options: list[WorkoutOption] = field(default_factory=list)
```

</details>

<details class="training-card-details">
<summary>WorkoutOption</summary>

```python
@dataclass(slots=True)
class WorkoutOption:
    title: str
    repeat: str = ""
    selection_notes: str = ""
    load_notes: str = ""
    parts: list[SessionPart] = field(default_factory=list)
```

</details>

<details class="training-card-details">
<summary>SessionPart</summary>

```python
@dataclass(slots=True)
class SessionPart:
    title: str
    prescription: str = ""
    duration: str = ""
    rpe: str = ""
    selection_notes: str = ""
    coaching_notes: str = ""
    terrain_notes: str = ""
    adjustment_notes: str = ""
```

</details>

#### Supporting Classes

The supporting classes help keep these fields consistent:

- `CardType` identifies whether a card is a *macro*, *mezzo*, *micro*, or *session* card. It keeps the hierarchy explicit.

- `TrainingLevel` describes which athletes the card is suitable for, from *beginner* to *elite*.

- `CardReference` stores a connection to another card, together with the type of relationship, such as *parent*, *child*, *alternative*, or *support*. It can also include small tags that add context to the connection.

<details class="training-card-details">
<summary>CardReference</summary>

```python
@dataclass(slots=True)
class CardReference:
    card_id: str
    relationship: CardRelationship
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
```

</details>

Using predefined values prevents small naming differences from representing the same thing and keeps the whole library consistent. Together, these supporting classes make the cards easier to filter, connect, and use later.
